---
title: "Module 2 --- Motor and transmission shaft"
---


## Summary

A brushless motor with a custom shaft pressed into its rotor bell, with the sun
gear and the sensor magnet installed, bolted to its bracket and mounted on the
motor plate. The motor is soldered to the electronic speed controller. The gearbox itself goes on in [Module 4](04-control.qmd).

## Requirements

| | |
|---|---|
| **Parts** | AS2303 KV1500 motor with pre-machined bell, custom motor shaft, sun gear from the Faulhaber 23.04:1 gearbox, 6 × 2.5 mm diametric magnet, 3D-printed magnet bracket, vertical nylon motor bracket, bottom fuselage plate, mounting screws |
| **Tools** | Circlip pliers, manual arbor press, superglue, hex drivers |
| **Read** | This page, and the *Motor shaft* section below in full before touching the motor. [Brushless motors](/reference/bldc.qmd) for the background |


## The motor --- AS2303 KV1500 {#sec-motor-variant}
The AS2303 is a **brushless outrunner**. Read
[Brushless motors](/reference/bldc.qmd) first.

![](/Fig/TMO-AS2303-1500.jpg){width=45%}

We use the AS2303 KV1500 motor throughout the course. Its propeller horn
**cannot** be separated from the bell, it has to be machined off in a lathe.
That work, and the custom shaft, are prepared before the session.

### What the KV rating means {#sec-kv}

**KV** is the motor's *velocity constant*, quoted in rpm per volt. It says how
fast the rotor spins per volt applied, **with no load on the shaft**:

$$\omega_0 = k_V \, U$$ {#eq-kv}

The constant is not a marketing number --- it falls out of the motor's
physics. As the rotor turns, its magnets sweep past the windings and induce a
voltage that opposes the supply (the *back-EMF*):

$$U_\text{emf} = \frac{\omega}{k_V}$$ {#eq-bemf}

The supply voltage splits between this back-EMF and the ohmic drop across the
winding resistance $R$, so $U = U_\text{emf} + R\,I$ and the speed under load
becomes

$$\omega = k_V \left( U - R\,I \right)$$ {#eq-loaded}

which is why @eq-kv only holds at $I \approx 0$. Draw current and the motor
slows down.

The same constant fixes the torque. Electrical power in equals mechanical power
out, $U_\text{emf} I = \tau \omega$, and substituting @eq-bemf gives
$\tau = I / k_V$ in SI units. Converting $k_V$ from rpm/V to rad/s/V:

$$k_T = \frac{60}{2\pi \, k_V} \approx \frac{9.55}{k_V}
\qquad \text{with} \qquad \tau = k_T \, I$$ {#eq-kt}

with $k_T$ in N·m/A when $k_V$ is in rpm/V. **Torque and speed constants are
inverses of each other.** A high-KV motor spins fast but gives little torque
per amp; a low-KV motor of the same size and mass does the opposite. Both
cannot be had at once --- the choice is where to sit on that trade-off, and
then to recover the missing torque with a reduction.

### What this means for our robot

With $k_V = 1500$ rpm/V and a 4S LiPo at its 14.8 V nominal voltage:

$$\omega_0 = 1500 \times 14.8 = 22\,200 \ \text{rpm}
\qquad
k_T = \frac{9.55}{1500} = 6.4 \ \text{mN·m/A}$$

6.4 mN·m/A is very little torque, too little to drive the wings
directly, which is exactly why the 23.04:1 Faulhaber gearbox is there. It
multiplies torque by 23.04 and divides speed by the same factor. One revolution
of the gearbox output is one full flapping cycle, so

$$f_\text{flap} = \frac{\omega}{60 \, r}
= \frac{22\,200}{60 \times 23.04} = 16.1 \ \text{Hz}$$ {#eq-fflap}

at no load. Under real aerodynamic and hydrodynamic loading the drive tops out
near 15 200 rpm, i.e. about **11 Hz** of flapping, the figure that reappears
in [Module 4](04-control.qmd).

## Motor shaft

To pair the motor with the gearbox, the stock shaft of the brushless motor is
replaced by a custom one. What is left to
do is the disassembly and the press fit, which is still a delicate operation:
the motor's structure is mostly aluminium and quite thin, for weight savings.

1. Remove the circlip on the shaft with the special pliers. **Don't lose it,
   nor the brass ring.**

2. Separate the rotor from the stator delicately, by hand.

3. Press the stock shaft out of the rotor bell.

   ::: {.callout-warning}
   ## Never load the bell radially

   Press the shaft out very carefully, making sure to never apply forces
   radially on the bell. Use the manual press with appropriate support below
   the bell to avoid deforming the dome shape. **Do not squeeze the bell with a
   vice, or even by hand.**
   :::

4. Press the sun gear onto the new shaft.

   ::: {.callout-warning}
   ## Sun gear first --- this order cannot be undone

   The sun gear goes on **while the shaft is still free**. Once the shaft is
   pressed into the bell, it can no longer be supported properly to press the
   gear on.
   :::

5. Press the new shaft into the bell, making sure not to press on the
   dome-shaped part of the bell without appropriate support underneath. It is a
   **tight fit** on the bell and a **clearance fit** through the bearings.

![Motor shaft dimensions](/Fig/shaft_drawing.png){#fig-motor-shaft width=70%}

## Sensor magnet

The AS5047P encoder wired up in [Module 3](03-esc.qmd) does not touch the
shaft. It reads the direction of the magnetic field from a small magnet
rotating in front of it, so the magnet has to go on the motor.

Use a **6 × 2.5 mm diametrically magnetised disc magnet**. *Diametrically* magnetised is the part that matters:
the poles are across the diameter, not through the thickness, so the field seen
by the sensor sweeps through a full rotation as the shaft turns. An ordinary
axially magnetised disc of identical size presents the same pole to the sensor
all the way round and gives no angle at all.

1. Drop the magnet into its recess in the 3D-printed bracket. It should sit
   flat, fully seated, with no rocking.

2. **Centre it on the axis of rotation.** The bracket locates it, but check. Keep the magnet concentric with the
   shaft to within **0.5 mm**.

3. Bond it with **a single drop of superglue**. One drop is enough.

4. Turn the assembly through a full revolution by hand and watch the magnet.
   Any visible wobble means it is off-centre or not seated.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Off-centre magnets are hard to diagnose later

An eccentric magnet may still produces a perfectly plausible angle reading at times.
:::

## Mounting the motor

With the shaft and the magnet done, the motor goes onto the robot plate. This happens
in two stages: motor to bracket, then bracket to plate.

1. Fix the motor to the vertical **3D-printed nylon bracket** using **four
   screws M2x5 mm** through the mounting holes in the motor base. Don't over tighten. Check that the rotor still turns freely by hand. Nylon is compliant, and
   overtightening can pull the bracket out of flat enough to preload the
   bearings. A motor that spun freely on the bench and feels stiff once bolted
   down needs the screws backed off and retightened more gently.

3. Mount the bracket to the **bottom fuselage plate**. Before tightening,
   check the orientation: the shaft and sun gear must point towards the front of the robot.

![Motor and ESC](/Fig/motor_with_esc.jpg){#fig-motor-with-shaft width=70%}

## Solder the motor wires to the Electronic Speed Controller
Since the pads are large, make sure to use enough heat / large tip on the soldering iron. The order of the cables UVW do not matter.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Watch this before picking up the iron
[Soldering Crash Course: Basic Techniques, Tips and Advice](https://youtu.be/6rmErwU5E-k)
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Checkpoint

Shaft seated with the sun gear on it, the rotor spinning freely by hand with no
wobble, the magnet bonded concentric to within 0.5 mm, and the motor bolted to
its bracket and mounted on the plate - still turning freely once bolted down.
:::
